17 Appendix #4 Segmentation and Block Aggregation 17.1 Introduction The term “block” is often used in many different ways, but in Patchworks, it has a very specific meaning. In Patchworks terminology a block: is the smallest spatial unit in the Patchworks model; may consist of one or more polygons from the original inventory that have been dissolved together; is either a simple or multi-part polygon that has a single feature to describe its geographical location; serves as a “building block” for creating harvest areas. The scheduler may choose multiple adjacent blocks to create a harvest area; is relatively homogeneous for silviculture; may be composed of managed areas (productive landbase eligible for treatments) and/or unmanaged areas (protected forest or other areas of concern); is indivisible: treatments are applied uniformly across the entire managed area of a block. Before being used by Patchworks, the original GIS inventory is usually overlaid with buffers, wildlife areas, and other areas of concern, resulting in the creation of many smaller sliver polygons. It would be unrealistic to consider allocating management treatments to these small slivers, and a common data preparation step is to aggregate or group polygons together into candidate blocks. In the grouping process, the objective is to form blocks that are of a size, shape, and composition that make sense to operational planners as realistic units of allocation. One approach for develop spatially coherent management units within Patchworks is to use a graph-based blocking framework based on select forest inventory attributes and local spatial connectivity relationships. The approach represents the forested landscape as a network in which individual raster cells are treated as nodes and neighbouring cells are linked through spatial adjacency. Similarity between adjacent cells is quantified using multiple forest attributes including stand age, height, basal area, and volume, which are standardized and combined into a multivariate distance metric. This allows both forest condition and spatial contiguity to influence the formation of block aggregates. The resulting framework groups neighbouring cells with similar structural characteristics into contiguous patches while preserving boundaries between substantially different forest conditions. As a prototype, the method provides a means of generating ecologically and operationally meaningful planning blocks that may serve as an alternative or complement to traditional polygon-based stratification approaches within Patchworks. 17.2 Methods The graph-based raster segmentation algorithm partitions a spatial dataset into groups of similar and connected pixels by representing the raster as a graph. Each raster cell is treated as a vertex (node) and spatial adjacency between neighbouring cells is represented as an edge. The objective of the algorithm is to identify contiguous regions whose cells are more similar to one another than to cells in neighbouring regions. Rather than relying solely on geographic proximity, graph-based segmentation incorporates both spatial connectivity and attribute similarity, allowing the landscape to be divided into ecologically meaningful segments. In forest applications, the resulting segments can be interpreted as relatively homogeneous patches of forest structure and composition that are connected in space. To quantify similarity between adjacent cells, a multivariate quadratic distance metric is assigned to each graph edge. Each forest cell is described by a vector of standardized attributes based on stand height, basal area, age, and volume. For every pair of adjacent cells, a difference vector is calculated and used to compute a quadratic distance of the form: dTWd where d is the vector of attribute differences and W is a weighting matrix. When W is an identity matrix, the metric simplifies to a squared Euclidean distance, giving equal importance to each forest attribute. Small distances indicate neighboring cells with similar forest characteristics, while large distances indicate abrupt changes in stand structure or composition. The weighted graph produced by this procedure provides the foundation for segmentation. Edges with low weights represent strong ecological similarity and tend to be retained within segments, whereas edges with high weights represent boundaries between dissimilar forest conditions and are more likely to be cut during the segmentation process. The algorithm therefore groups adjacent cells into contiguous regions that minimize within-segment variability while maximizing differences among segments. The resulting forest patches can be used to characterize structural heterogeneity, identify management units, assess landscape connectivity, or examine the spatial distribution of forest conditions across the landscape. 17.2.1 Set-up Using the Soo TSA as our example landscape we start by creating a 1 ha. gridded dataframe of the analysis forest with four attributes,age,height,volume and basal area. The scale() function standardizes each variable by first centering it and then scaling it. Centering subtracts the mean of each attribute (e.g., Height, Basal Area, Age) from every value so that the variable has a mean of zero, effectively expressing each observation as its deviation from the landscape average. Scaling then divides these centered values by the variable’s standard deviation, giving each variable a standard deviation of one. The result is a set of unitless z-scores that place all attributes on a common scale, ensuring that variables with larger numeric ranges (such as Age) do not dominate subsequent analyses such as clustering, PCA, or distance calculations. The order is important: centering occurs first to remove differences in variable means, followed by scaling to normalize differences in variability. Positive z scores values indicate observations above the dataset mean, while negative values indicate observations below the mean. In the subset shown below,most stands have above-average age values (approximately 1.04 standard deviations above the mean), while basal area and volume vary between moderate and high positive standardized values,suggesting differences in stand stocking and productivity among otherwise similar-aged stands. The resulting edges matrix stores each pair of adjacent cells that will be compared. The adjacent() function from the terra package was used to identify neighbouring forest raster cells. Using 8-directionconnectivity, the function returned pairs of adjacent cell IDs, creating an edge list that describes the spatial connectivity among forest cells. This edge list was subsequently used to construct a graph representation of the landscape for connectivity and network analyses. The argument pairs = TRUE instructs the adjacent() function to return neighboring raster cells as pairs of connected cell identifiers. Each row of the resulting output represents a connection between two adjacent cells, forming an edge list that can be used directly to construct a graph and analyze landscape connectivity using network-based metrics. Code mask<- aflb values(mask) <- NA values(mask)[tsa31_df$cell] <- 1 # Forest cell IDs in the original raster forest_cells <- which(values(mask) == 1) adj <- adjacent( #from to List of cell ids mask, cells = forest_cells,#only assess forest cells directions = 8,#queens case pairs = TRUE ) edges <- as.matrix(adj) 17.2.4 Convert Raster Cell IDs to X Row IDs The adjacency relationships generated from the raster were first converted to a matrix (edges), where each row represents a connection between two neighboring forest cells, and the total number of graph edges was calculated as the number of rows in this matrix. Because the feature matrix X contains one row for each forest cell rather than the original raster cell identifiers, a lookup table (cell_to_row) was created to map raster cell IDs to their corresponding row numbers in X. This lookup was then used to replace the raster cell IDs in the edge list with the appropriate row indices from X, producing a new edge list (edges_X) that directly references observations in the standardized dataset. Finally, any edges containing unmatched or missing values were removed using complete.cases(), ensuring that the resulting graph structure contained only valid connections between forest cells represented in X and could be used reliably for subsequent connectivity and network analyses. For every connected pair of neighboring forest cells identified in the graph, a difference vector (D) was calculated by subtracting the standardized attribute values of one cell from those of its adjacent neighbour. Each row of D therefore represents the multivariate dissimilarity between two connected stands across all four variables. Because the variables were standardized beforehand, differences among variables are measured on a common scale, preventing attributes with larger original units or ranges from disproportionately influencing the analysis. The difference vectors were then used to compute edge weights using the quadratic form dTWd , where d is the difference vector for a given edge and W is the weighting matrix. Since W is the identity matrix, the quadratic form simplifies to the squared Euclidean distance between neighboring cells in the four-dimensional standardized feature space. 17.2.5.1 Example Calculation of Edge Weight Consider two adjacent forest cells with standardized attributes: Variable Cell A Cell B Height 0.50 1.00 Basal Area 1.20 0.70 Age -0.30 -0.10 Volume 0.80 0.20 The difference vector is: \[d = \begin{bmatrix} -0.5 \\ 0.5 \\ -0.2 \\ 0.6 \end{bmatrix}\] Using an identity weighting matrix \[W = I\] the quadratic distance becomes \[d^T W d = (-0.5)^2 + (0.5)^2 + (-0.2)^2 + (0.6)^2\] \[= 0.25 + 0.25 + 0.04 + 0.36\] \[= 0.90\] Therefore, the edge connecting these two neighboring forest cells receives a weight of 0.90, representing their multivariate dissimilarity in standardized age, height, basal area, and volume. Larger weight values indicate greater differences in stand structure and composition between adjacent forest cells, while smaller values indicate greater similarity. Any edges producing missing weight values were identified and removed, and the corresponding rows were excluded from both the edge list (edges_X) and the weight vector (weights). This ensured that the final graph contained only valid connections with well-defined measures of ecological dissimilarity for use in subsequent connectivity, clustering, or graph-based analyses. Code # Equal weighting of all 4 variables W <- diag(4) # Difference vectors for every edge D <- X[edges_X[,1], ] - X[edges_X[,2], ] # Quadratic form: d'Wd # For W = I this reduces to squared Euclidean distance weights <- rowSums((D %*% W) * D) # Remove edges with NA weights valid <- !is.na(weights) edges_X <- edges_X[valid, ] weights <- weights[valid] summary(weights) ## Min. 1st Qu. The calculated quadratic distances were assigned to the graph as edge weights (E(g)$weight), allowing each connection to reflect the degree of structural dissimilarity between adjacent stands based on standardized height, basal area, age, and volume attributes. Code g <- graph_from_edgelist( edges_X, directed = FALSE ) E(g)$weight <- weights 17.2.7 Segmentation This code performs graph-based landscape segmentation by removing edges that connect structurally dissimilar neighboring cells. The threshold is defined as the 50th percentile of the edge-weight distribution, where edge weights represent the standardized differences in Height, Basal Area, and Age between adjacent cells. All graph connections with dissimilarity values greater than this threshold are deleted, leaving only the strongest structural similarities intact. The threshold determines the maximum level of multivariate dissimilarity that can exist between adjacent cells while still allowing them to be grouped into the same segment. Lower threshold values produce many small, highly homogeneous segments by retaining only the strongest similarity connections, whereas higher threshold values allow more dissimilar cells to connect and merge into larger segments. The resulting graph (g_segmented) breaks into connected components that represent spatially contiguous groups of cells with similar forest structure, effectively partitioning the landscape into homogeneous forest patches separated by pronounced structural boundaries. The Minimum Mapping Unit (MMU) filter identifies forest segments that are smaller than a specified minimum area threshold, which in this case is 5 hectares. After assigning each forest cell to a segment and calculating segment areas, the code selects all segments whose area is less than the MMU, flagging them as small segments that may be too small to be operationally or analytically meaningful. The number of segments below the MMU is then reported, providing an indication of how many small, potentially fragmented patches may require merging with adjacent segments or removal in subsequent processing.
